edition: Issue 034: Martha's 'awareness' costume, the Cup's 5pm calendar veto, and New Zealand's first bank with zero branches
tagline: Your 3-minute Tuesday reset, served before the 5pm Melbourne Cup deletes every calendar in the country: one billionaire costume apology, one race that stops a nation, one bank with no lamingtons at the counter.

stories.headline: The Melbourne Cup runs today at 5pm NZ time: no NZ-trained horses, two NZ-bred hopes, and a favourite racing 13 years of history
stories.summary: The 2026 Melbourne Cup runs at Flemington today at 5pm NZ time, with British gelding Point of Law the favourite and two NZ-bred runners - Asterix, part-owned by former Black Cap Mark Greatbatch, and Waikato-bred Shockletz - flying the flag for a country with no NZ-trained horse in the 24-horse field.

body.text: The race that stops a nation runs today, and New Zealand's office productivity is expected to take its annual hit at 5pm NZ time when 24 horses go around at Flemington. British gelding Point of Law - a 3-year-old sired by unbeaten Frankel and winner of the Geelong Cup on 21 October - rocketed to favourite after Saturday night's barrier draw, jumping from barrier nine under jockey Ethan Brown at 53kg. The only other runner at single-figure odds on the NZ TAB as of Monday was Ireland's Trustyourinstinct, one of five Joseph O'Brien runners, ridden by Kiwi-expat James McDonald. There are no New Zealand-trained horses in the field this year, but two New Zealand-bred runners: Asterix (#9, Chris Waller/Jye McNeil, 55kg), bred by Sir Owen Glenn's Go Bloodstock and owned by a Kiwi syndicate that includes former Black Cap Mark Greatbatch, and Shockletz (#24, Ciaran Maher/Harry Coffey, 51kg), bred at Waikato's Rich Hill Stud. The winner collects A$4.8 million from a A$10.2 million prize pool - the world's richest handicap - plus an 18-carat gold trophy.

Every year we do this: the nation's single largest collective act of financial recklessness is a $5 sweepstakes entry, which New Zealand law thoughtfully caps at $5000 so no office in the country can involve a mortgage. No NZ-trained horses this year, so the flag rests on Asterix - a comic-book Gaul part-owned by a cricketer - and Shockletz, whose name sounds like the weather alert that cancels your Tuesday. And spare a sympathetic thought for the bookies' eternal optimism: the last Cup favourite to actually win was Fiorente in 2013, which means Point of Law is carrying 13 years of disappointed punters' baggage into barrier nine. But whatever the result, the real winner is already locked in: between 5.00 and 5.05 every 'meeting' on every calendar will mysteriously relocate to the break room, and absolutely nobody will ever work out what happened.

RNZ (2 Nov 2026, 'Melbourne Cup race time, horses, favourites, winners and predictions: What you need to know'): race runs Tuesday 3 November at Flemington, 5pm NZ time, over 3200m (shortened from 3219m in 1972). No NZ-trained horses in the 24-runner field. NZ-bred runners: Asterix (sire Tavistock, bred by Sir Owen Glenn's Go Bloodstock, owner group includes former Black Cap Mark Greatbatch, won the 2022 NZ Derby, trained by Chris Waller, ridden by Jye McNeil) and Shockletz (sire Shocking, bred at Waikato's Rich Hill Stud, trained by Ciaran Maher, Harry Coffey rides unless replaced by Kiwi-expat Michael Dee after Coffey injured his shoulder in a weekend fall). Prize money A$10.2 million (world's richest handicap), winner earns A$4.8 million plus the 18-carat gold trophy. NZ law caps sweepstakes at $5000. The last favourite to win the Cup was Fiorente in 2013. Last NZ-bred winner: Verry Elleegant (2021); last NZ-owned and trained winner: Ethereal (2001). NZ Herald (2 Nov 2026, 'Melbourne Cup 2026: Field, sweepstake, odds, tips, history'): Point of Law is a 3-year-old sired by unbeaten Frankel, won the Geelong Cup on 21 October, barrier 9 with Ethan Brown at 53kg; barrier draw conducted at Flemington on Saturday night; Kingston Rule holds the race record of 3min 16.3sec (1990); the race used to be two miles before the metric change in 1972.

stories.headline: Martha Stewart apologises for her 'awareness' Halloween costume: a homelessness get-up, a candle plug, and the year's most tone-deaf caption
stories.summary: America's first self-made female billionaire posted then deleted an Instagram photo of herself dressed as a homeless person holding an 'I AM HUNGRY HELP ME!!' sign - with a caption promoting her candle collection. After a backlash that drew 'let them eat cake' comparisons, she apologised twice, admitting the costume was 'insensitive and not funny'.

body.text: Martha Stewart has apologised - twice - after a Halloween post that sparked what one critic called the year's most tone-deaf costume. In a since-deleted Instagram photo, the TV personality, author and America's first self-made female billionaire appeared dressed as a homeless person: black hat, distressed jeans, cardigan, black marks smeared across her face, holding a sign reading 'I AM HUNGRY HELP ME!!' - with a caption promoting her candle collection. Critics were quick, with one invoking Marie Antoinette: 'What in the let them eat cake is this costume?' Stewart first told Page Six on Sunday the look was 'intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness', then later issued a longer apology on Instagram: 'It's hard to admit when you've really screwed up... Wearing a costume like I did was insensitive and not funny. I am very sorry.' More than 700,000 people are homeless in the United States, according to official data.

Let's be clear about target selection before we start: the joke is not the 700,000 people without a home. The joke is the person who looked at that statistic and thought 'costume material'. 'It was meant to raise awareness' is the official hymn of wealthy people being caught being wealthy, and Martha performed it to a standing ovation - the sign demanded help, the caption offered candles, and the only thing that went hungry was the algorithm. Tucked inside the backlash was the single most devastating sentence of the year: 'what in the let them eat cake is this costume' - economics served as a roast. Credit where it's due, though: the second apology - 'insensitive and not funny. I am very sorry' - is short, correct and contains no mention of awareness, which is basically billionaire growth. The candle, we assume, will be reissued as 'Homelessness Support: notes of cardboard and regret'.

RNZ (Amarachi Orie, 3 Nov 2026, 'Martha Stewart says she really screwed up with homeless Halloween costume'): Stewart's costume - black hat, distressed jeans, cardigan, black marks on her face, and a sign reading 'I AM HUNGRY HELP ME!!' - appeared in a since-deleted Instagram post whose caption promoted her candle collection; the report describes her as America's first self-made female billionaire. One critic called it 'the most tone-deaf Halloween costume' of the year; another called the post 'grotesque, disgusting, morally bankrupt, incredibly wrong' and asked 'What in the let them eat cake is this costume?'. Stewart told Page Six on Sunday the costume was 'intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness'; RNZ notes more than 700,000 people are homeless in the US per official data. Later that day she apologised on Instagram: 'It's hard to admit when you've really screwed up... I know many people are suffering economically. Wearing a costume like I did was insensitive and not funny. I am very sorry.' CNN has reached out to her representatives for further comment. In August, Target apologised and stopped selling a Halloween costume critics said evoked blackface and minstrel shows.

stories.headline: Revolut becomes a registered bank in NZ: first digital bank, a $120m commitment, credit cards inbound - and no branch to queue in
stories.summary: UK fintech Revolut (valued at up to US$214 billion pre-IPO) launched as New Zealand's first registered digital bank on Tuesday with a promised $120m local investment, telling Kiwis its upcoming credit cards will finally deliver 'responsible lending' that leaves 'legacy banking delays in the past'.

body.text: Revolut launched as a registered bank in New Zealand on Tuesday after securing regulatory approval, backed by a commitment to invest $120 million in the local market - and it comes with a claim no branch-based bank has yet made on its own behalf. The London-founded app company, which has operated here for about three years, becomes New Zealand's first digital bank, with credit card products promised 'in the coming months'. 'When we roll credit cards out in the coming months, Kiwis will finally experience a frictionless, paperless, data-driven, and responsible lending process that leaves legacy banking delays in the past,' CEO Ryan Brosnahan said. The launch follows Revolut's December 2024 application to become a registered NZ bank - part of an expansion plan RNZ reported involved further investment of $120 million and roughly tripling local staff - and Stuff reported last month that Revolut sees New Zealand's concentrated banking market as 'ripe for disruption', citing a pre-IPO valuation of up to US$214 billion and the company's title sponsorship of the Audi Formula One team.

A bank with no branches, no queues and no lamingtons at the counter is now officially A Bank, and it would like you to know its lending is 'frictionless, paperless, data-driven and responsible' - four words never before arranged in one sentence about banking by anyone who has read a terms-and-conditions page. The disruption war has peaked: on one side, the challenger with a US$214 billion valuation and a Formula One sponsorship; on the other, the incumbents with a century of free pens. Somewhere between 'the market is ripe' and 'delays are in the past' sits the actual experience of borrowing money, which remains, history suggests: wait, wait, form, wait. But credit where it's due - with the word 'registered' attached, a Revolut deposit now carries the full weight of the government behind it, which is a meaningful step up from being an app with a market cap. Brave new world, delivered entirely from a phone, with customer support arriving, like the legacy delays, shortly.

BusinessDesk (Andy Macdonald, 2 Nov 2026, 'Revolut secures bank registration'), surfaced on the NZ Herald homepage (3 Nov): Revolut launched as a registered bank in New Zealand on Tuesday 3 November after securing regulatory approval, backed by a commitment to invest $120 million locally; described as NZ's first digital bank, with credit cards to roll out 'in the coming months'; CEO Ryan Brosnahan is quoted on the 'frictionless, paperless, data-driven, and responsible lending process' that 'leaves legacy banking delays in the past'. Corroborating context: RNZ (Dec 2024, 'Banking platform Revolut looks to more than double NZ staff numbers') reported Revolut's application to become a registered NZ bank and plans to invest a further $120m and nearly triple local staff; Stuff (Grant Bradley, 23 Oct 2026, 'Revolut says NZ banking sector is ripe for disruption') reported Revolut launched in NZ about three years ago, sees the concentrated NZ banking market as ideal for its model, has a pre-IPO valuation of up to US$214 billion, and holds title sponsorship of the Audi Formula One team. Source-rule note: the launch itself is carried by BusinessDesk via the NZ Herald homepage rather than a native NZ Herald/Stuff/RNZ report; flagged for human review.
